arXiv:2608.09696v5 [cs.AI] 27 Sep 2026

Model Discovery Agent:
LLM-assisted Bayesian experiment design for data-efficient discovery of mechanistic world models

Kevin Murphy Affiliation: Dept. Computer Science Affiliation: Univ. British Columbia, Canada.
September 27, 2026
Abstract

A primary goal of science is to learn mechanistic world models from limited experimental data, both to explain observations and to predict novel interventions. We introduce the Model Discovery Agent (MDA), which combines LLM proposals for ℳ\mathcal{M}-open model discovery, experiment design based on Value of Information, and approximate Bayesian inference over model structures, parameters, and stochastic latent trajectories. We apply MDA to learn symbolic reaction rate laws for ChemBench (Kabra et al., 2026), partially observed ODE models for GlucoseBench (Xie, 2018; Kovatchev et al., 2009), and partially observed SDE models for a new stochastic single-neuron simulator we create. In the appendix, we also show results on various other domains from BoxingGym (Gandhi et al., 2025). We show that MDA has improved sample efficiency compared to various baseline methods, and the learned models are good predictors but also provide interpretable abstractions of each domain.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we develop a new algorithm for learning a mechanistic world model (aka causal world model) from a small amount of data.11 1 We use the term “mechanistic world model” following (Posner et al., 2026). These are models composed of modular, scientifically meaningful building blocks or mechanisms, as in a structural causal model (Pearl, 2009). In this paper, we restrict ourselves to “level 2” causality (Bareinboim et al., 2022); this can be handled with standard decision-theoretic machinery (Dawid, 2015; Mlodozeniec et al., 2025), and does not need the more complex machinery required for “level 3” counterfactual reasoning (Dawid, 2000). Note that the philosophy of science literature makes a distinction between causal models and mechanistic models (see e.g., (Machamer et al., 2000; Craver, 2006; Woodward, 2004; Weber, 2008; Glennan, 2017; Batterman & Rice, 2014)); we use the term mechanistic broadly here. Such models can support scientific explanation and prediction (Salmon, 1984; Shmueli, 2010; Krenn et al., 2022; Messeri & Crockett, 2024; Bajorath, 2025; Serre & Pavlick, 2025; Kramer et al., 2026; Posner et al., 2026). In addition, they can be used to answer interventional questions (Pearl, 2009; Richens & Everitt, 2024): not “what will happen?” but “what would happen if I did action aa?” (e.g., predicting the effect of administering a new drug to a patient).

Unfortunately, a model with latent variables/ mechanisms is typically unidentifiable from observation alone: the passive data underdetermines it, and interventions — perturbing the system and watching how it responds — can distinguish explanations that passive data cannot. But experiments are expensive (a lab assay, a clinical trial), which makes the operative problem data efficiency: identify the model, well enough to answer future queries, in as few experiments as possible. This is the classical remit of Bayesian experimental design (BED) — choose the intervention whose outcome is most informative (Lindley, 1956; Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995; Rainforth et al., 2024) — increasingly combined with hypothesis generation in recent active theory-learning systems (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024; Elteto et al., 2026; Prystawski et al., 2026). Here we study this combination across explicit algebraic models and partially observed deterministic and stochastic dynamics.

We define this problem formally in Section 2. Then in Section 3 we present a solution, which we call the Model Discovery Agent (MDA), which combines three ingredients: approximate Bayesian inference over a hierarchy of models, parameters, and latent trajectories, implemented using particle methods or MAP estimation; a large language model (LLM), which is used as a way to propose new models when the current hypothesis space is detected to be insufficient (this is needed to tackle the ℳ\mathcal{M}-open regime, where the true model may lie outside the current hypothesis class (Bernardo & Smith, 1994; MacKinlay, 2016; Kelter, 2020)); and an experiment designer based on maximizing the Value of Information (see e.g., (Rainforth et al., 2024)). The loop fits and weights candidate models, selects an experiment, and uses predictive discrepancies to guide further proposals.

In Section 4, we empirically evaluate MDA on problems of increasing complexity, and compare to various baselines. On ChemBench (Kabra et al., 2026), MDA discovers static symbolic rate laws for chemical reactions. On GlucoseBench (Xie, 2018; Kovatchev et al., 2009), MDA learns partially observed deterministic ODEs, including latent compartments that encode delayed input responses. Finally, on NeuronBench, a novel single-neuron electrophysiology benchmark we introduce based on a stochastic version of the Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) model, MDA learns a partially observed SDE. In the appendix (Appendix E), we also report results of applying MDA to BoxingGym (Gandhi et al., 2025), which contains a variety of simple problems from psychology to ecology, which we model using Generalized Linear Models and probabilistic programs. Across these benchmarks, MDA discovers interpretable models which provide strong predictive performance on novel inputs and interventions.

2 Problem statement

Agent-environment interface.

We consider an agent interacting with an unknown “blackbox” dynamical system (c.f., (Ljung, 1998)). The outputs or observations are y1:Ty_{1:T}, for yt∈𝒴⊂ℝdyy_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}. The inputs or control signals a1:Ta_{1:T} are chosen by the agent using at∼π(⋅∣a1:t−1,y1:t−1,t)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid a_{1:t-1},y_{1:t-1},t), with at∈𝒜⊂ℝdaa_{t}\in\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}, where π\pi is the policy.22 2 For interventional prediction, we assume actions depend only on recorded history and context (including state estimates computed from them), with policy randomization independent of system noise. This excludes unmeasured confounding of action selection; causal identification additionally requires adequate action coverage and suitable model/identification assumptions (Cornish et al., 2026). Without these, same-policy observational prediction may still be accurate, but need not transfer to a new intervention or policy. The agent can also optionally specify the initial condition of the system, z0z_{0}; if it is not specified, its distribution must be inferred from the training data and context. Finally, the agent can optionally apply a perturbation or intervention δ\delta that modifies the system parameters, yielding θ′=do⁡(δ,θ)\theta^{\prime}=\mathrm{do}(\delta,\theta). (An omitted perturbation leaves the system unchanged.) We define an experiment design as the tuple χ=(δ,z0,π)\chi=(\delta,z_{0},\pi).

Experimental protocol.

The agent is presented with some background context CC, and an optional initial dataset 𝒟0={(χi,y1:Ti):i=1:N0}\mathcal{D}_{0}=\{(\chi^{i},y_{1:T}^{i}):i=1:N_{0}\}, where each sample is drawn from the system using y1:Ti∼p∗(⋅|χi)y_{1:T}^{i}\sim p^{\ast}(\cdot|\chi^{i}). (We also record the sampled inputs a1:Tia_{1:T}^{i}, but omit this from notation, for brevity.) The agent is then given a budget of KK turns to interact with the system. At each step, it designs an experiment χk=(δk,z0k,πk)\chi^{k}=(\delta^{k},z_{0}^{k},\pi^{k}), records one trajectory (episode) y1:Tky_{1:T}^{k} from the environment, and updates 𝒟0:k=𝒟0∪{(χi,y1:Ti):i=1:k}\mathcal{D}_{0:k}=\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\{(\chi^{i},y_{1:T}^{i}):i=1:k\}. The agent can use this data to update its beliefs about the underlying model, pk(m)=p(m∣C,𝒟0:k,ℳk)p_{k}(m)=p(m\mid C,\mathcal{D}_{0:k},\mathcal{M}_{k}), where the candidate support ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} may grow or shrink, and this belief can be used to design the next experiment, and to make predictions about the future. The objective is low held-out forecasting loss within the experiment budget; MDA uses model-discrimination information gain as a tractable acquisition surrogate (Eq. 59), not the held-out outcomes themselves. See Algorithm 1 for the pseudocode for this experimental protocol, that is agnostic to the form of the agent.

Conditional forecasting and evaluation.

We evaluate predictions on held-out experiments, not recovery of a unique true mechanism, since distinct latent models can have similar interventional predictions (Beckers & Halpern, 2019; Dyer et al., 2023; Cornish et al., 2026). Given a new design, χ∼𝒬\chi\sim\mathcal{Q}, the oracle rolls out the policy to collect the ground truth trajectory (a1:T,y1:T)(a_{1:T},y_{1:T}). Let tct_{c} be a cut point, through which the agent observes the initial history ℋtc=(a1:tc,y1:tcobs)\mathcal{H}_{t_{c}}=(a_{1:t_{c}},y_{1:t_{c}}^{\rm obs}), including observation masks when entries are missing. (If tc=0t_{c}=0, the agent does not see any such prefix.) The agent must then predict a distribution over (functions of) future observables, given this partial history ℋtc\mathcal{H}_{t_{c}}, the training data 𝒟=𝒟0:k\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{0:k}, and any relevant context or metadata CC, by computing the posterior predictive distribution:33 3 If χ\chi specifies an open-loop policy π\pi, then it defines the whole input sequence a1:Ta_{1:T} up front (so the policy is just a function of time, not the past observations or actions). If π\pi is a closed-loop policy, then future inputs atc+1:Ta_{t_{c}+1:T} must be generated jointly with future observations ytc+1:Ty_{t_{c}+1:T}, when forecasting the future. (This paper focuses on learning action-conditioned world models, not on learning the policy of another agent from observational data.)

p(F(Ytc+1:T)∣χ,ℋtc,𝒟,C).p\!\left(F(Y_{t_{c}+1:T})\mid\chi,\mathcal{H}_{t_{c}},\mathcal{D},C\right). (1)

The target function FF maps the future observation sequence to a scalar, feature vector, or trajectory, depending on the benchmark. For ChemBench it is the scalar log-rate F⁡(y)=log⁡(1+y)∈ℝF(y)=\log(1+y)\in\mathbb{R}, matching nMSLE; for GlucoseBench it is the future observed trajectory F(ytc+1:T)=ytc+1:T∈ℝ(T−tc)​dyF(y_{t_{c}+1:T})=y_{t_{c}+1:T}\in\mathbb{R}^{(T-t_{c})d_{y}}, where dy=2d_{y}=2 is the number of observed variables per step; and for NeuronBench, it is a vector of summary features, F(y1:T)∈ℝ6F(y_{1:T})\in\mathbb{R}^{6} (e.g., neuron spike count — see Eq. 90 for details). We condition on the observed history so far ℋtc\mathcal{H}_{t_{c}} for this unit (if tc>0t_{c}>0), plus the training episodes 𝒟0:k\mathcal{D}_{0:k} (collected by the agent), plus any supplied context or metadata CC.

We mostly focus on predicting the mean of Eq. 1, and measuring performance with squared error, although we do consider distributional forecasting metrics in Section D.2. In the simplest setting, where the prediction target is the raw observation sequence, F(y1:T)=y1:TF(y_{1:T})=y_{1:T}, there is no missing data, and tc=0t_{c}=0 (so there is no history prefix), the normalized mean squared error metric we use is

LnMSE=1dy​∑i=1dy∑q=1Q∑t=1T(y^q​t​i−yq​t​i)2N​si2L_{\rm nMSE}=\frac{1}{d_{y}}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{y}}\frac{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\hat{y}_{qti}-y_{qti})^{2}}{Ns_{i}^{2}} (2)

Here qq indexes held-out queries (novel experiments/designs), ii observation channels, tt future time points, yq​t​iy_{qti} is the observation. y^q​t​i\hat{y}_{qti} is the agent’s prediction, sis_{i} is a scaling factor that is benchmark specific, and N=Q​TN=QT is the number of observed time points in the test set. We give the general case in Section A.2.

3 Method

Overview.

The MDA method is visualized in Fig. 5; see Algorithm 2 for detailed pseudocode. At each step, the agent updates its belief state pk=p(m|𝒟0:k)p_{k}=p(m|\mathcal{D}_{0:k}), which is a posterior distribution over models or hypotheses mm, represented as a weighted finite set. MDA then chooses the next experiment by maximizing the value of information, χk+1=arg⁡maxχ∈𝒳​VoI​(χ,pk)\chi_{k+1}=\arg\max_{\chi\in\mathcal{X}}\text{VoI}(\chi,p_{k}). It runs the experiment and updates its dataset by appending 𝒟k+1\mathcal{D}_{k+1}. After KK rounds, the agent is asked to forecast the outcomes to some novel experimental conditions. We describe this in more detail below, but for full details, see Appendix A.

The three-level hierarchy.

In the general case, MDA represents the unknown world by the 3 level hierarchy corresponding to the State Space Model shown in Fig. 1. In equations, this corresponds to

m∼p⁡(m),θ∼p⁡(θ∣m),θ′=do⁡(δ,θ)\displaystyle m\sim p(m),\qquad\theta\sim p(\theta\mid m),\qquad\theta^{\prime}=\mathrm{do}(\delta,\theta) (3)
zt∼pm​(zt∣zt−1,at;θ′),yt∼pm​(yt∣zt;θ′),\displaystyle z_{t}\sim p_{m}\!\left(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t};\theta^{\prime}\right),\qquad y_{t}\sim p_{m}(y_{t}\mid z_{t};\theta^{\prime}), (4)

for t=1:Tt=1{:}T, with z0z_{0} specified by χ\chi when available (otherwise assigned an initial-state distribution), and ata_{t} selected by π\pi. The discrete structure mm specifies what the latent variables ztz_{t} are, and how they depend on each other, as well as the functional forms for all the distributions; θ\theta specifies the numerical parameters; z1:Tz_{1:T} is the latent trajectory; and y1:Ty_{1:T} is what is measured. MDA must perform inference over structures, parameters, and —when dynamics or initial states are uncertain—latent paths.

Computing the posterior over models.

The belief state over models, pk=p(m|𝒟0:k)∝p(m)p(𝒟0:k∣m)p_{k}=p(m|\mathcal{D}_{0:k})\propto p(m)p(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}\mid m), is represented as a discrete distribution over a finite candidate pool. This is computed using Bayes’ rule over the models in the pool, and then keeping the top NmN_{m}, if a cap on pool size is imposed.

Expanding the hypothesis space.

Bayes rule can move probability mass between different models in its current hypothesis class. However, in the ℳ\mathcal{M}-open case (Bernardo & Smith, 1994; Kelter, 2020), we acknowledge that our initial hypothesis class may be insufficient to capture the truth, so we need a way to grow it on demand. To do this, we compute a predictive check, i.e., we evaluate the performance of the current best model on a novel (input,output) pair (c.f., (Kelter, 2020)), and/or check the fit on all the currently collected data. If the error is too large, MDA expands the hypothesis space by prompting the LLM to suggest one or more novel models conditioned on the observations and context. Where available, the prompt also includes the current model pool and residual diagnostics. Note that this hypothesis expansion step is the only part of MDA that uses an LLM. After expanding the pool of models, we compute the evidence for each new model and renormalize, keeping the top NmN_{m} models. Crucially, we do not require the LLM to propose the right model in a single shot; instead, it can suggest local mutations to previous hypotheses, and thus can iteratively refine the candidate library by performing RmR_{m} iterations of expansion, scoring and pruning. See Algorithm 2 for details.

Shrinking the hypothesis space.

If the highest model weight is sufficiently high, and if its error is sufficiently low, then we can optionally shrink the pool down to a minimal size, by adapting the value of NmN_{m}. This limits computational cost and candidate proliferation. Shrinkage is gated by confidence and fit quality, but can still discard a model that becomes useful later. Maintaining a diverse library of hypotheses is important, even if the posterior is very concentrated on just a single model, since it improves the search process, similar to other evolutionary optimization algorithms such as FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024).

Computing the marginal likelihood (evidence).

To compute the posterior over models, we need to estimate the marginal likelihood or evidence for each model, Zmk=p(𝒟0:k|m)=∫p(𝒟0:k|m,θ)p(θ|m)dθZ_{m}^{k}=p(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}|m)=\int p(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}|m,\theta)\,p(\theta|m)\,d\theta, where the likelihood factorizes over the trajectories: p(𝒟0:k|m,θ)=∏i∈𝒟0:kp(y1:Ti|χi,m,θ)p(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}|m,\theta)=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0:k}}p(y_{1:T}^{i}|\chi^{i},m,\theta). We estimate ZmkZ_{m}^{k} using tempered SMC in Section A.6.1 or the BIC approximation in Section A.6.3. The Bayesian evidence averages the likelihood over the declared parameter prior (MacKay, 1991), which provides an automatic Occam penalty that depends on both model flexibility and the parameter prior. However, for some problems we also add an explicit complexity penalty by using the model prior p⁡(m)∝e−λ​Cmp(m)\propto e^{-\lambda C_{m}}, where CmC_{m} is the number of free parameters in mm and λ\lambda is tuned on a validation set. (By default we use λ=0\lambda=0, corresponding to a uniform prior.)

Computing the likelihood.

For latent variable models, computing the likelihood of a single trajectory, p(y1:T∣χ,m,θ)=∫∏t=1Tp(yt∣zt,m,θ)p(zt∣zt−1,at,m,θ)dz1:Tp(y_{1:T}\mid\chi,m,\theta)=\int\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(y_{t}\mid z_{t},m,\theta)\,p(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t},m,\theta)\,dz_{1:T}, may be intractable. For this we mostly use another layer of SMC, namely the bootstrap particle filter in Section A.5.1, although we also compare to the Bayesian Synthetic Likelihood method in Section A.5.2.

Experiment design.

We choose the experiment whose outcome is most informative about which hypothesis is true: χ⋆=arg⁡maxχ∈𝒳⁡I⁡(M;Yχ∣𝒟)\chi^{\star}=\arg\max_{\chi\in\mathcal{X}}I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D}) (Lindley, 1956; Box & Hill, 1967; Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995; Rainforth et al., 2024). This is called the Expected Information Gain (EIG), which is a special case of Value of Information (VoI). In practice we use the model-disagreement surrogate in Eq. 59, which is an approximation to the mutual information. We optimize the VoI surrogate using CMA-ES (Hansen, 2016) for ChemBench, which has 7 real-valued inputs, and exact enumeration of finite action menus for GlucoseBench and NeuronBench. See Section A.9 for details.

Prediction.

After each step, we convert the belief state, which is a distribution over models, pk=p(m|𝒟0:k)p_{k}=p(m|\mathcal{D}_{0:k}), to a predictive distribution in observation space, ρk(χ)=p(Y|χ,𝒟0:k)\rho_{k}(\chi)=p(Y|\chi,\mathcal{D}_{0:k}), which is computed by Bayes model averaging (c.f., (Self & Cheeseman, 1987)). From this, we derive the posterior predicted mean of the target, which is optimal under the ℓ2\ell_{2} loss we use in Eq. 2:

F^k(χ)=𝔼[F(Y)|χ,𝒟0:k]=∑m∫[∫F(y)p(y|m,θ,χ)dy]p(m,θ|𝒟0:k)dθ\displaystyle\hat{F}_{k}(\chi)=\mathbb{E}[F(Y)|\chi,\mathcal{D}_{0:k}]=\sum_{m}\int\Big[\int F(y)\,p(y|m,\theta,\chi)\,dy\Big]\,p(m,\theta|\mathcal{D}_{0:k})\,d\theta (5)

For conditional forecasting (where tc>0t_{c}>0), the inner predictive distribution also conditions on the query prefix in Eq. 1; this can be implemented by estimating the latent state at the forecast cut point tct_{c}. We also consider simplifications of this, where we just plugin the MAP model m^k\hat{m}_{k} and its corresponding parameters, θ^k\hat{\theta}_{k}, instead of averaging over them. For F⁡(y)=yF(y)=y, the prediction becomes the plugin posterior predictive mean F^k(χ)=𝔼[Y∣m^k,θ^k,χ]\hat{F}_{k}(\chi)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\hat{m}_{k},\hat{\theta}_{k},\chi]. For general target functions, we can sample from the posterior predictive, and then approximate E⁡[F⁡(Y)]E[F(Y)] by Monte Carlo.

4 Experimental results

We organize the results by order of increasing model complexity. ChemBench requires fitting static symbolic laws; glucose forecasting requires learning partially observed deterministic ODEs; and NeuronBench requires prediction from partially observed SDEs. In each case we evaluate held-out interventional prediction. We plot test performance vs the total number of experiments at each step kk, which is Bk=N0+kB_{k}=N_{0}+k, where N0N_{0} are the number of initial experiments in 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}. The final MDA budgets are 3+223+22, 2+42+4, and 2+82+8 in chemistry, glucose, and HH, respectively. Additional results, on BoxingGym, can be found in Appendix E.

Baselines.

We compare MDA to two main classes of baseline. The first class are methods based on induction, which fit a model (m^,θ^)(\hat{m},\hat{\theta}) given 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and then predict using this model. For ChemBench, we use the method from their paper, and for GlucoseBench, we fit ARX and sparse polynomial dynamics (SINDYc). We also consider two baseline approaches based on transduction, which use an LLM to directly predict the output YY given the test input χ\chi and all the training data 𝒟\mathcal{D}, i.e., they ask the LLM to generate arg⁡maxy⁡p⁡(y∣χ,𝒟)\arg\max_{y}p(y\mid\chi,\mathcal{D}) using in-context learning (ICL). Surprisingly, (Li et al., 2024b) showed that the transductive approach can outperform the inductive approach on some ARC AGI problems, so this is not a trivial baseline.44 4 Induction and transduction use compute in different ways. For induction, most of the time is spent in numerical model fitting, and the LLM calls (for proposing new models) are only a small fraction of the overall time. (The model fitting uses CPUs, which we run locally on a laptop or sometimes on Modal; the LLM calls (which we access via OpenRouter) use hardware accelerators of various forms, such as GPUs.) For transduction, all of the time is spent inside the LLM. It is therefore hard to match compute budgets. However, our focus in this paper is on sample efficiency, not compute effiency. to The experiments used to create the data 𝒟\mathcal{D} can either be chosen by the LLM itself (which we call “ICL (+LLM design)”, c.f., (Gupta et al., 2025)), or by the MDA agent (which we call “ICL (+MDA design)”); this distinction isolates the effects of experiment design from prediction.

LLMs.

We use GPT-5.6-Luna at medium reasoning effort as our LLM for all the agents used in the main paper (except the LLM-free ARX baseline for GlucoseBench). However, some older results in the appendix (in particular, the BoxingGym results in Appendix E), used Claude-Opus-4.7. We have not systematically studied the effects of LLM choice due to cost, and since this is orthogonal to the concerns of this paper. None of the agents have internet access, or the ability to read source code or data files. Prompts are in Appendix G.

4.1 ChemBench: discovering enzyme-kinetic rate laws

Benchmark.

ChemBench is derived from (Kabra et al., 2026). The task is to learn a static algebraic law mapping seven controllable inputs—substrate, inhibitor, second-substrate and product concentrations, enzyme loading, temperature, and pH—to the initial rate of a chemical reaction:

r=f⁡(CA,CI,CB,CP,E,T,pH,θ).r=f(C_{A},C_{I},C_{B},C_{P},E,T,\mathrm{pH};\theta).

The complete benchmark contains 57 worlds: nine canonical mechanisms and 48 compound mechanisms. We use the medium difficulty level for all worlds. We evaluate held-out prediction error using RMSLE, as defined in Eq. 67, and its normalized nMSLE version, as defined in Eq. 68. An agent is said to “pass” a given world if 𝟙[RMSLE<0.05]\mathbbm{1}[\mathrm{RMSLE}<0.05]. See Appendix B for further details.

Methods.

MDA is initialized with three scalar rate observations in 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}, which are created by varying CA∈{0.03,0.3,3}C_{A}\in\{0.03,0.3,3\} and holding the other terms constant. It then actively selects K=22K=22 additional experiments. We initialize the hypothesis space with nine canonical mechanisms plus up to 12 valid, nonduplicate LLM proposals; later triggered calls request six candidates, with a live-pool cap of 24. We fit each model by bounded, multistart nonlinear least squares, and approximate the marginal likelihood using the BIC approximation in Eq. 45. We approximate the model posterior using p(m∣𝒟)∝e−BICm/2p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\propto e^{-\mathrm{BIC}_{m}/2}. The predictor uses the highest-weight model and its point estimate θ^m\hat{\theta}_{m}. Experiment design uses the derivative-free CMA-ES algorithm of (Hansen, 2016) to maximize the weighted between-model disagreement in Eq. 69, which is an approximation to EIG. (See Fig. 7 for some evidence that these EIG designs outperform random designs.) For the main baseline, we use the LLM-AutoSciLab agent from (Kabra et al., 2026), which combines an LLM with the evolutionary symbolic regression method PySR (Cranmer, 2023), independently fitted at each budget B∈{5,10,15,20,25}B\in\{5,10,15,20,25\}. For the ICL+MDA baseline, we reuse MDA’s data, and for ICL+LLM, we start with 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} but then use the LLM to choose the next 22 experiments.

Results.

Figure 2(a) shows that MDA is substantially more sample efficient than the other methods. (The small error spike at B=10B=10 for LLM-AutoSciLab is explained in Section B.3.) Figure 2(b) visualizes the posterior over models over time created by MDA on a specific example, along with the corresponding test error. At steps 6 and 15, an inadequate fit triggers an expansion of the hypothesis space; the second such expansion adds the orange model, and its selection sharply reduces error. Illustrative laws from MDA and LLM-AutoSciLab are shown in Table 1.

4.2 GlucoseBench: discovering latent ODE models

Benchmark.

GlucoseBench modifies simglucose (Xie, 2018), a Python implementation of the UVA/Padova type-1 diabetes model (Kovatchev et al., 2009). The original simulator was FDA-accepted for preclinical insulin-control testing in place of animal trials (Cobelli & Kovatchev, 2023). Its 30 virtual patients (ten per age group) have hidden 13-dimensional nonlinear ODE states. Agents observe noisy glucose every five minutes and insulin every 15 minutes over six hours; simulator variables and parameters remain hidden. After two initial episodes, agents select four more from 48 meal amount/time and bolus amount/delay templates. We evaluate twelve unseen interventions for the same patient, conditioned on a 45-minute prefix; other cuts and details appear in Appendix C.

Methods.

MDA starts with four compartment ODEs and can add mechanisms and latent states (up to six per model). It fits parameters numerically, weights models using BIC (Eq. 45), and selects experiments with noise-normalized disagreement (Eq. 77). An EKF conditions states on the query prefix before BIC-weighted prediction (Eq. 76). Baselines are the two ICL methods, an ARX model for each observation channel (Section C.3), and SINDYc sparse polynomial dynamics (Brunton et al., 2016a; Brunton et al., 2016b). ARX and SINDYc are fitted to MDA’s data, since they cannot desgin their own experiments. Each patient is fitted separately (a single shared model is future work).

Results.

Figure 3(a) shows that MDA is much more sample efficient than the other methods in terms of predicting future GCM given a prefix of tc=45t_{c}=45 minutes (see Fig. 8 for the effect of changing the prefix length). Figure 3(b) illustrates a 6-state model learned by MDA after 3 trajectories. It shows the sparse latent connectivity and added memory nodes, which retain the effects of transient inputs.

4.3 NeuronBench: discovering mechanisms with stochastic latent dynamics

Benchmark.

NeuronBench is a new benchmark we created based on generalized stochastic Hodgkin–Huxley models. Each world uses one of six “mystery neurons”, five with nonstandard mechanisms and one with a textbook M-current comparator. Finite populations of ion channels introduce intrinsic gating noise, turning the hidden voltage-and-gate dynamics into an SDE. The agent observes 20 noisy voltage samples per experiment. The design space consists of 90 structured electrical pulse protocols which specify the input current over time. We score held-out predictions using a six-dimensional functional F(y1:T)F(y_{1:T}) containing spike-count, adaptation, run-down, and sub-threshold voltage features, defined in Eq. 90. See Appendix D for further details.

Methods.

A model mm specifies which ion-channel mechanisms are present, parameters θ\theta include their conductances and kinetics, and the latent path z1:Tz_{1:T} contains voltage and unobserved channel gates. We consider 4 MDA variants: stochastic dynamics (SDE) vs deterministic dynamics (ODE), crossed with recursive SMC estimation of the parameter posterior and evidence (Section A.6.2) vs MAP parameter estimation plus the BIC evidence approximation (Section A.6.3). The ODE arms use the Gaussian likelihood in Eq. 24, and the SDE arms estimate the likelihood with a bootstrap particle filter (Section A.5.1); the likelihood is then used as input to SMC parameter posterior estimation or parameter point estimation. We also compare to the two ICL baselines.

Results.

Figure 4(a) shows that MDA with stochastic dynamics (and either SMC or BIC estimate for marginal likelihood) works much better than deterministic ODE approximations, and both work better than the two ICL baselines. Figure 4(b) shows that stochastic sample paths retain spiking variability that the fitted ODE misses. These predictions do not exactly match the precise spike times of the single sample ground truth rollout, but they suffice to get low nMSE score of 0.38 for the feature summary (aggregated over 24 queries) for the SDE+SMC method, compared to 7.41 for the ODE+BIC method.

5 Related work55 5 For more related work, see Appendix F.

  • •

    Causal models for interventional prediction. Predicting “what if” questions using causal models is discussed at length in Pearl (2009). Recently Richens & Everitt (2024) established a theoretical connection between robust prediction over a rich intervention class and causal models; however, our finite held-out tests do not establish causal identification. There is also much recent work on causality and LLMs (see, e.g., Kıcıman et al., 2024; Ban et al., 2025). We choose to use an LLM to explicitly represent causal mechanisms, rather than performing implicit reasoning, since a key goal is to discover an interpretable model. Our model-based pipelines outperform the tested ICL forecasters, but also use numerical fitting and simulation; this is not a compute-matched isolation of induction versus transduction.

  • •

    Bayesian experimental design. Choosing the most informative experiment is the classical model-discrimination objective of (Lindley, 1956), reviewed in (Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995; Rainforth et al., 2024; Huan et al., 2024). Recently (Choudhury et al., 2026) proposed to combine BED with LLMs, but our approach is very different, since we use the LLM to propose an explicit probabilistic model, whereas they perform all probability calculations implicitly using the LLM itself.

  • •

    LLMs for scientific discovery. LLMs have been used to fit scientific models to static datasets, often augmented with literature review, using blackbox optimization (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Wahl et al., 2026; Kasenberg et al., 2026; Aygün et al., 2026; Gottweis et al., 2026; Xie & Wilson, 2026; Song et al., 2025). In addition there is some work on actively collecting datasets for model fitting using agent-designed experiments (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Abhyankar et al., 2026; Elteto et al., 2026; Prystawski et al., 2026; Jagadish et al., 2026; Bisht et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al., 2026). MDA builds on SMC-S’s pool-conditioned symbolic proposals (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024) and shares mechanistic population scoring with ModelSMC (Wahl et al., 2026). ATLAS (Elteto et al., 2026) similarly uses active discrimination among RNN hypotheses to recover agents in bandit tasks. Our emphasis is a common executable-model interface across algebraic, ODE, and stochastic latent-dynamics tasks, with controlled inference and acquisition comparisons (see Appendix F for SINDy and other numerical approaches).

  • •

    Benchmarks for interactive scientific discovery. Various benchmarks evaluate agents that learn scientific laws by interactive experimentation: we build on ActiveSciBench-Chem (Kabra et al., 2026), and BoxingGym (Gandhi et al., 2025), and add a glucose study and our own NeuronBench. Other relevant benchmarks include DiscoverPhysics (Wiemann et al., 2026), NewtonBench (Zheng et al., 2026), Science-Gym (Cerrato et al., 2026), and SciGym (Duan et al., 2025).

6 Discussion

MDA combines LLM-proposed executable libraries with approximate Bayesian inference and experimental design, to learn models with predictively useful abstractions. In the future we would like to improve inference efficiency, using methods such as amortized SBI (Cranmer et al., 2020; Radev et al., 2022; Deistler et al., 2025), as well as tackle harder benchmarks by giving the LLM more tools for analysing data (rather than putting everything in the prompt) and for proposing a library of reusable model mechanisms.

7 AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to help write the code, launch and analyse experiments, and help with writing and figure preparation.

Appendix A Method: further details

A.1 The agent-environment interface

Algorithm 1 sketches the agent/environment interface at a high level.77 7 Our API is loosely based on BoxingGym’s Fig. 2 (Gandhi et al., 2025). However, we make several changes: (i) we evaluate after every step, to get a learning curve, rather than a single number; (ii) we add an update-state method to each agent, since MDA sequentially updates its belief state.

A.2 Evaluation

Let P^q\hat{P}_{q} be the agent’s predictive distribution for query qq, conditional on χq\chi_{q}, its observed prefix ℋtc,q\mathcal{H}_{t_{c,q}}, training data 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and context CC. The squared-error point prediction is

f^q=𝔼P^q[F(Ytc,q+1:T)].\hat{f}_{q}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}_{q}}[F(Y_{t_{c,q}+1:T})]. (6)

For nonlinear features, this is 𝔼⁡[F⁡(Y)]\mathbb{E}[F(Y)], not F⁡(𝔼⁡[Y])F(\mathbb{E}[Y]). Write its entries as f^q​j​i\hat{f}_{qji}, where i=1,…,dFi=1,\ldots,d_{F} indexes feature components, or observed channels for trajectory targets (then dF=dyd_{F}=d_{y}); jj indexes future times and is a singleton for a scalar or fixed-dimensional feature vector. In general we use the following normalized mean squared error metric:

LnMSE=1dF​∑i=1dF∑q,joq​j​i​(f^q​j​i−fq​j​iref)2Ni​si2,Ni=∑q,joq​j​i.L_{\rm nMSE}=\frac{1}{d_{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{F}}\frac{\sum_{q,j}o_{qji}(\hat{f}_{qji}-f^{\rm ref}_{qji})^{2}}{N_{i}s_{i}^{2}},\qquad N_{i}=\sum_{q,j}o_{qji}. (7)

Here qq indexes held-out queries (novel experiments/designs), ii observation channels or feature dimensions, jj future time points (a singleton for scalar or feature targets), oo is an observation mask (all ones when fully observed), with Ni>0N_{i}>0 for each scored component, and sis_{i} is a scaling factor that is benchmark specific. (Chemistry specifies sis_{i} in Eq. 68; Glucose specifies sis_{i} in Eq. 73; HH specifies sis_{i} in Eq. 91.) f^q​j​i\hat{f}_{qji} is the agent’s prediction, and fq​j​ireff_{qji}^{\rm ref} is a reference, corresponding to an observed outcome or an independently estimated oracle mean, as specified by the benchmark. For a fully observed fixed-dimensional feature vector, this becomes

Lfeatures=1dF​∑i=1dF∑q(f^q​i−fq​iref)2Q​si2L_{\rm features}=\frac{1}{d_{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{F}}\frac{\sum_{q}(\hat{f}_{qi}-f^{\rm ref}_{qi})^{2}}{Qs_{i}^{2}} (8)

For trajectory targets, this becomes

Ltraj=1dy​∑i=1dy∑q∑t>tc,qoq​t​i​(y^q​t​i−yq​t​i)2si2​∑q∑t>tc,qoq​t​i\displaystyle L_{\rm traj}=\frac{1}{d_{y}}\sum_{i=1}^{d_{y}}\frac{\sum_{q}\sum_{t>t_{c,q}}o_{qti}(\hat{y}_{qti}-y_{qti})^{2}}{s_{i}^{2}\sum_{q}\sum_{t>t_{c,q}}o_{qti}} (9)

For univariate fully observed time series of common length TT, with tc=0t_{c}=0 and s1=1s_{1}=1, this simplifies further to the familiar expression

Ltraj=1Q​T​∑q=1Q∑t=1T(y^q​t−yq​t)2\displaystyle L_{\rm traj}=\frac{1}{QT}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\hat{y}_{qt}-y_{qt})^{2} (10)

For probabilistic forecasts, we can go beyond evaluating the mean by scoring the full predictive distribution P^q\hat{P}_{q}, which may integrate uncertainty over states, parameters, and model structures. The reference distribution Pq⋆P_{q}^{\star} is the oracle’s distribution for the same target, design, and observed prefix. CRPS scores a univariate forecast against a held-out realization (or is averaged over independent oracle draws), which we discuss in Section D.2.

A.3 Main MDA loop

Overview.

The MDA algorithm is shown schematically in Fig. 5. It is a sequential Bayesian experiment-design loop, where we use an LLM to propose model structures; but every numeric quantity — the parameter posterior, the marginal evidence, the model posterior p⁡(m∣𝒟)p(m\mid\mathcal{D}), the VoI design score, and the forecast — is computed by numerical fitting, inference, and acquisition routines, never by the LLM. See Algorithm 2 for the high level pseudocode; we will describe the individual functions below.

SSM.

The agent assumes the unknown environment can be represented by the state-space model defined in Eqs. 4 and 1.88 8 The SSM assumption is without loss of generality, since any non-Markovian model can be converted to Markov form, as long as the latent state space is allowed to grow. An experiment design χ\chi is the choice of initial state z0z_{0}, the policy π\pi (a fixed input sequence a1:Ta_{1:T} in our open-loop experiments) and the optional perturbations δ\delta. We use the following notation: θ′=do⁡(δ,θ)\theta^{\prime}=\mathrm{do}(\delta,\theta) are the parameters of the system after applying intervention δ\delta, ztz_{t} are the hidden states, ata_{t} are the optional inputs, and yty_{t} are the observed outputs. For simpler models, there might not be any latent variables — equivalent to z=constz=\text{const} — or there might not be any temporal dynamics — equivalent to T=1T=1.

Latent dynamics.

For a fixed open-loop input sequence, the distribution over latent paths is given by

p(z1:T|χ,θ,m)=∏t=1Tp(zt|zt−1,χ,θ′,m)\displaystyle p(z_{1:T}|\chi,\theta,m)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(z_{t}|z_{t-1},\chi,\theta^{\prime},m) (11)

Here the formula conditions on z0z_{0} when specified by χ\chi; otherwise integrate over its declared initial-state distribution. The same convention applies to the compact likelihood algorithms below. Query prediction additionally conditions on its observed prefix, with ℋ=∅\mathcal{H}=\varnothing when tc=0t_{c}=0. Note that p⁡(zt|zt−1,at,θ)p(z_{t}|z_{t-1},a_{t},\theta) may be an implicit distribution, that we can sample from but cannot evaluate pointwise. For some cases, the latent dynamics are deterministic, and are given by an ODE:

p⁡(zt∣χ,θ,m,z0)\displaystyle p(z_{t}\mid\chi,\theta,m,z_{0}) =δ⁡(zt−zt​(χ,m,θ))\displaystyle=\delta(z_{t}-z_{t}(\chi,m,\theta)) (12)
zt​(χ,m,θ)\displaystyle z_{t}(\chi,m,\theta) =ODE-solve(t,m,θ′,z0,a1:t)\displaystyle=\text{ODE-solve}(t,m,\theta^{\prime},z_{0},a_{1:t}) (13)

where θ′\theta^{\prime} are the (optionally perturbed) parameters, z0z_{0} is the initial condition specified by χ\chi, and a1:Ta_{1:T} are the inputs specified by its open-loop policy.

Observation model.

We usually assume the emission distribution is

p⁡(yt|zt,m,θ)=𝒩⁡(yt|fo​(zt),σ2)\displaystyle p(y_{t}|z_{t},m,\theta)=\mathcal{N}(y_{t}|f_{o}(z_{t}),\sigma^{2}) (14)

where fof_{o} is the observation model. For scalar latent state space, this is often the identity function; for multivariate latent state space (e.g., as in HH), fof_{o} often is a linear projection, which selects the relevant observable components.

Three-level inference.

MDA has to deal with 3 levels of unknowns: the latent states z1:Tz_{1:T} (where we may have T=1T=1 for static systems), the parameters θ\theta, and the model structure m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. Bayesian inference at the top level requires that we compute

p⁡(m∣𝒟,ℳ)=p⁡(𝒟∣m)​p​(m)p⁡(𝒟)=p⁡(𝒟∣m)​p​(m)∑m′∈ℳp⁡(𝒟∣m′)​p​(m′)\displaystyle p(m\mid\mathcal{D},\mathcal{M})=\frac{p(\mathcal{D}\mid m)p(m)}{p(\mathcal{D})}=\frac{p(\mathcal{D}\mid m)p(m)}{\sum_{m^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}}p(\mathcal{D}\mid m^{\prime})p(m^{\prime})} (15)

This is computed by the model-posterior function in Algorithm 9. When we add the hypothesis space expansion procedure of Algorithm 12, we get a method that is similar to the SMC-S procedure discussed in Section A.8.

To compute the marginal likelihood or evidence Zm=p⁡(𝒟∣m)Z_{m}=p(\mathcal{D}\mid m), we have to marginalize out the parameters:

p⁡(𝒟∣m)=∫p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ)​p​(θ∣m)​𝑑θ\displaystyle p(\mathcal{D}\mid m)=\int p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\theta)p(\theta\mid m)d\theta (16)

By default, this is computed using tempered SMC in Algorithm 6. See Section A.6 for details.

Finally, to compute the (observed data) likelihood, we have to marginalize out the latents:

p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ)=∫p⁡(𝒟∣z,m,θ)​p​(z∣m,θ)​𝑑z\displaystyle p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\theta)=\int p(\mathcal{D}\mid z,m,\theta)p(z\mid m,\theta)dz (17)

By default, this is computed by bootstrap particle filtering (a special case of SMC) in Algorithm 4. See Section A.5 for details.

Using PF to estimate p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ)p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\theta) inside of an outer SMC algorithm to estimate p⁡(θ∣𝒟,m)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D},m) follows the nested architecture of SMC2 (Chopin et al., 2013). Our outer level enumerates and weights candidate models rather than running another SMC sampler. The three-level hierarchy thus combines particle inference within models with approximate finite-library selection; LLM proposals and pruning search for useful structures.

Simpler inference backends.

If the latent variables are missing, or can be computed deterministically, then we don’t need the bottom-most PF layer to compute the likelihood. For the finite candidate pool, model weights are computed by enumeration; there is no additional structure-level SMC layer. We also consider other approximations, such as replacing particle filtering for computing the likelihood with Bayesian synthetic likelihood (see Section A.5.2), and replacing tempered SMC for computing the marginal likelihood with a BIC approximation (see Section A.6.3).

From beliefs to actions.

Given a posterior p⁡(m,θ|𝒟)p(m,\theta|\mathcal{D}), we can choose the next experiment χ\chi by maximizing the value of information provided by χ\chi, as explained in Section A.9.

From beliefs to predictions.

Given a posterior p⁡(m,θ|𝒟)p(m,\theta|\mathcal{D}), we can predict the outcome of a novel experiment using the posterior mean:

F^BMA​(χ)=∫∫∑mF⁡(Y)​p​(Y|χ,m,θ)​p​(m,θ|𝒟)​𝑑Y​𝑑θ\displaystyle\hat{F}_{\mathrm{BMA}}(\chi)=\int\int\sum_{m}F(Y)p(Y|\chi,m,\theta)p(m,\theta|\mathcal{D})dYd\theta (18)

We also consider a simplified prediction, where we use a plugin estimate with the MAP model and its parameters,

F^plugin​(χ)=∫F⁡(Y)​p​(Y|χ,m^,θ^m)​𝑑Y\displaystyle\hat{F}_{\mathrm{plugin}}(\chi)=\int F(Y)p(Y|\chi,\hat{m},\hat{\theta}_{m})dY (19)

where θ^m\hat{\theta}_{m} is the posterior mean or mode of the parameters for model m^\hat{m}.

Experimental settings.

Table 2 summarizes the different variants of MDA that we use in our main experiments. Further details can be found in the following appendices.

A.4 Priors

Candidate structures may be seeded or LLM-proposed; each has its own free parameters θ\theta. The joint prior factorises as

p⁡(m,θ)=p⁡(m)​∏j=1Cmp⁡(θj∣m),\displaystyle p(m,\theta)=p(m)\,\prod_{j=1}^{C_{m}}p(\theta_{j}\mid m), (20)

with a uniform prior on each coefficient over its declared bounds99 9 When the proposer chooses bounds after seeing data, those bounds define a data-dependent prior. Conditioning on that choice does not remove data reuse: narrowing bounds around a fit can inflate evidence. These are approximate predictive model weights, not calibrated Bayes factors under a prespecified prior. , and a structure prior

p⁡(m)∝e−λ​Cm,\displaystyle p(m)\propto e^{-\lambda C_{m}}, (21)

where CmC_{m} is the number of free parameters of mm and λ\lambda is a per-parameter Occam penalty (in nats; the active per-domain settings and BIC exceptions are in Table 2). The posterior over structures is then p⁡(m∣𝒟)∝Zm​e−λ​Cmp(m\mid\mathcal{D})\propto Z_{m}\,e^{-\lambda C_{m}}, with Zm=∫p⁡(𝒟∣θ,m)​p​(θ∣m)​𝑑θZ_{m}=\int p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta,m)\,p(\theta\mid m)\,d\theta the marginal likelihood computed by Algorithm 6. When ℳ\mathcal{M}-open expansion adds a new structure it enters with the same unnormalized prior e−λ​Cme^{-\lambda C_{m}} and the posterior is renormalized over the current finite pool; there is no separate catch-all mass, so the pool is always a self-normalized distribution on the visited finite support.

Prior choice and predictive weighting.

Uniform priors are convenient, but not noninformative: their bounds and parameterization can substantially affect marginal likelihoods and hence model weights (Llorente et al., 2022). A stronger justification would combine physical parameter scales with prior-predictive checks that simulated responses are plausible across relevant interventions. Sensitivity of model weights need not imply sensitivity of predictions when different mechanisms behave similarly; our empirical claims concern held-out prediction rather than calibrated probabilities of recovering the true mechanism. For this predictive objective, an alternative is to choose ensemble weights using cross-validated or genuinely pre-update predictive scores, rather than marginal likelihoods. Such weights would represent predictive utility, not posterior model probabilities; the refitted residuals used in our adequacy checks are not held-out validation scores. A prospective safeguard is to fix parameter ranges by mechanism and physical units before seeing outcomes, or to evaluate newly proposed bounds only on subsequent data. Finite-bound validation alone does not prevent evidence inflation. We leave a systematic investigation of prior choice, predictive robustness, and predictive weighting to future work.

A.5 Computing the likelihood

All three likelihood routines take (𝒟,m,θ)(\mathcal{D},m,\theta) and sum the log-likelihoods over experiments (χi,yi,1:Ti)∈𝒟(\chi_{i},y_{i,1:T_{i}})\in\mathcal{D}, assumed conditionally independent given (m,θ)(m,\theta) and their designs. Each experiment has its own initial state and input sequence; trajectories are not concatenated. The recursive evidence update passes a singleton dataset for each new experiment.

We assume the complete-data conditional likelihood for a single experiment is given by

p(y1:T|z1:T,χ,m,θ)=∏t=1T𝒩(yt|fo(zt),σ2)\displaystyle p(y_{1:T}|z_{1:T},\chi,m,\theta)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{N}(y_{t}|f_{o}(z_{t}),\sigma^{2}) (22)

where fof_{o} is the observation model. Marginalizing out the latent variables gives the observed-data likelihood:

p(y1:T|χ,m,θ)=∫p(y1:T|z1:T,χ,m,θ)p(z1:T|χ,m,θ)dz1:T\displaystyle p(y_{1:T}|\chi,m,\theta)=\int p(y_{1:T}|z_{1:T},\chi,m,\theta)p(z_{1:T}|\chi,m,\theta)dz_{1:T} (23)

If the latent dynamics are deterministic, the likelihood is tractable:

p(y1:T|χ,m,θ)=∏t=1T𝒩(yt|fo(zt(χ,m,θ)),σ2)\displaystyle p(y_{1:T}|\chi,m,\theta)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{N}(y_{t}|f_{o}(z_{t}(\chi,m,\theta)),\sigma^{2}) (24)

where zt​(χ,m,θ)z_{t}(\chi,m,\theta) is defined in Eq. 13. See Algorithm 3. By contrast, for the stochastic models, the path integral over z1:Tz_{1:T} is generally intractable, so we must use approximations, which we discuss below.

A.5.1 Particle filtering

Our default method is to use the bootstrap particle filter algorithm shown in Algorithm 4. It propagates weighted filtering particles for p(zt∣y1:t,m,θ)p(z_{t}\mid y_{1:t},m,\theta); sampling posterior paths additionally requires retained ancestry or smoothing. The displayed routine returns an unbiased approximation of the likelihood, given by

p^(y1:T∣m,θ)=∏t(1Nz∑j=1Nzwt(j))\displaystyle\hat{p}(y_{1:T}\mid m,\theta)=\prod_{t}\big(\tfrac{1}{N_{z}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{z}}w_{t}^{(j)}\big) (25)

where wtjw_{t}^{j} is the weight of particle jj. For details, see e.g. (Chopin & Papaspiliopoulos, 2020; Naesseth et al., 2019).

A.5.2 Bayesian synthetic likelihood

An alternative to PF is to replace the likelihood p(y1:T|m,θ)p(y_{1:T}|m,\theta) with an approximation

ps(s(y1:T)|m,θ)≈𝒩(s(y1:T)|μm,θ,Σm,θ)\displaystyle p_{s}(s(y_{1:T})|m,\theta)\approx\mathcal{N}(s(y_{1:T})|\mu_{m,\theta},\Sigma_{m,\theta}) (26)

where s(y1:T)s(y_{1:T}) is some summary feature vector derived from the trajectory, and μ\mu and Σ\Sigma are computed as described below. This approximates the density of the summary, not the raw-data density. This is useful when a per-time step observation model, p⁡(yt|zt,m,θ)p(y_{t}|z_{t},m,\theta), is not available (since this is a requirement of PF). In addition, using the summary features can provide robustness to model misspecification.

To estimate μ\mu and Σ\Sigma, we can use the “Bayesian Synthetic Likelihood” method of (Wood, 2010; Deistler et al., 2025), which proceeds as follows. For each candidate (m,θ)(m,\theta) we draw RR traces (z(r),y(r))∼p(z1:T,y1:T∣m,θ)(z^{(r)},y^{(r)})\!\sim p(z_{1:T},y_{1:T}\mid m,\theta), throw away zrz^{r}, and then estimate the likelihood using

μm,θ\displaystyle\mu_{m,\theta} =1R​∑rs⁡(y(r))\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{R}\textstyle\sum_{r}s(y^{(r)}) (27)
Σm,θ\displaystyle\Sigma_{m,\theta} =Cov^r​[s⁡(y(r))]+ε​I,\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_{r}\!\big[s(y^{(r)})\big]+\varepsilon I, (28)

with a small ridge ε\varepsilon for conditioning. See Algorithm 5 for the pseudocode. We can also replace the Gaussian with a normalizing flow model, a technique called neural likelihood estimation (Papamakarios et al., 2019).1010 10 NLE is not to be confused with neural posterior estimation (Greenberg et al., 2019), which trains an amortized inference network to compute p(m,θ|y1:T)p(m,\theta|y_{1:T}). However, this requires generating mm and θ\theta, both of which can be hard (especially if the model mm is code). See (Cranmer et al., 2020; Frazier et al., 2024) for more discussion.

Instead of manually specifying s(y1:T)s(y_{1:T}), we can also learn it from data. A simple approach, known as semi-automatic ABC (Fearnhead & Prangle, 2012; Jiang et al., 2017), proceeds as follows: draw prior samples {(θr,mr,zr,y1:Tr)}\{(\theta^{r},m^{r},z^{r},y^{r}_{1:T})\} from the model, then train a neural network regression model to predict mrm_{r} and θr\theta_{r} given sϕ(y1:T)s_{\phi}(y_{1:T}). For example, we can let sϕ(y1:T)s_{\phi}(y_{1:T}) be a 1D CNN applied to the time series following by global average pooling, and then pass this embedding into an MLP fw​(s)f_{w}(s) with two output heads, one for classifying mm and one for predicting the mean of θr\theta_{r}:

(m^,θ^)=(fwm(sϕ(y1:T)),fwθ(sϕ(y1:T)))\displaystyle(\hat{m},\hat{\theta})=(f^{m}_{w}(s_{\phi}(y_{1:T})),f^{\theta}_{w}(s_{\phi}(y_{1:T}))) (29)

We then pass sϕ(y1:T)s_{\phi}(y_{1:T}), corresponding to the final layer of the network, into the above BSL method to compute the likelihood, which is passed to SMC to compute the evidence ZmZ_{m}.

There are two problems with BSL. (1) It is not much faster than PF (see e.g., Fig. 19), since it still requires rolling out RR stochastic trajectories for every candidate (m,θ)(m,\theta). (2) The above approach to learning sϕ​(y)s_{\phi}(y) with a neural network requires predicting mm and θ\theta on the output, which is challenging if θ\theta has variable size and/or mm is a complex structure (such as a graph or program) and not just a discrete index. We can avoid both problems by using neural ratio estimation (see e.g., (Hermans et al., 2020; Durkan et al., 2020)), which trains a binary classifier (on forwards-sampled data) to approximate the likelihood-to-evidence ratio

rϕ(y,m,θ)=dϕ1−dϕ≈p(y1:T∣m,θ)p(y1:T),r_{\phi}(y,m,\theta)\;=\;\frac{d_{\phi}}{1-d_{\phi}}\;\approx\;\frac{p(y_{1:T}\mid m,\theta)}{p(y_{1:T})}, (30)

Once trained, we can use rϕ​(y,m,θ)r_{\phi}(y,m,\theta) in lieu of p⁡(y|m,θ)p(y|m,\theta) inside of tempered SMC, without needing rollouts at run time, solving problem (1). Also, this is a discriminative model that conditions on mm and θ\theta and emits a scalar, avoiding variable-dimensional outputs. It still requires an encoding of (m,θ)(m,\theta) and simulation training coverage; generalization to newly proposed structures is not automatic. We leave exploration of this approach to future work.

A.6 Computing the marginal likelihood

To compare models with different numbers of parameters, we need to marginalize out their parameters by computing the evidence:

Zmk=p(𝒟0:k∣m)=∫p(𝒟0∣m,θ)[∏j=1kp(yj,1:T∣χj,m,θ)]p(θ∣m)dθZ_{m}^{k}=p(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}\mid m)=\int p(\mathcal{D}_{0}\mid m,\theta)\left[\prod_{j=1}^{k}p(y_{j,1:T}\mid\chi_{j},m,\theta)\right]p(\theta\mid m)\,d\theta (31)

where p⁡(y∣m,θ)p(y\mid m,\theta) is the observed data likelihood computed above.

A.6.1 Tempered SMC

Our default method to compute ZmkZ_{m}^{k} is to use tempered SMC with an adaptive tempering schedule, as shown in Algorithm 6. This also returns the posterior over the parameters for each model:

p(θ|m,𝒟0:k)≈∑i=1NpWikδ(θ−θi)\displaystyle p(\theta|m,\mathcal{D}_{0:k})\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N_{p}}W_{i}^{k}\delta(\theta-\theta_{i}) (32)

Refitting on all accumulated data at every experiment makes the total cost O⁡(K2​T​Np)O(K^{2}TN_{p}) per model, holding the tempering and rejuvenation budgets fixed and assuming an O⁡(T)O(T) trajectory likelihood. With PF likelihoods, this additionally scales with NzN_{z} (and the number of solver substeps per observation). The recursive alternative below avoids repeatedly processing old trajectories.

With noisy PF likelihoods, generally 𝔼⁡[L^β]≠Lβ\mathbb{E}[\widehat{L}^{\beta}]\neq L^{\beta} for 0<β<10<\beta<1. Unbiased PF estimates alone therefore do not justify the intermediate tempered targets; exact pseudo-marginal inference requires an appropriate extended-state construction (Andrieu & Roberts, 2009). We treat the implemented particle evidence as a numerical approximation.

A.6.2 Recursive parameter and evidence updates

For many experiments or long trajectories, full-history refitting is expensive. For a fixed model mm, define the new-experiment likelihood Lm,k(θ)=p(yk,1:T∣χk,m,θ)L_{m,k}(\theta)=p(y_{k,1:T}\mid\chi_{k},m,\theta). Conditioning on the chosen designs and assuming experiments are independent given (m,θ)(m,\theta), Bayes’ rule gives the exact recursion

cm,k\displaystyle c_{m,k} =∫Lm,k(θ)p(θ∣m,𝒟0:k−1)dθ,\displaystyle=\int L_{m,k}(\theta)\,p(\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D}_{0:k-1})\,d\theta, Zmk\displaystyle Z_{m}^{k} =Zmk−1​cm,k,\displaystyle=Z_{m}^{k-1}c_{m,k}, (33)
p(θ∣m,𝒟0:k)\displaystyle p(\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D}_{0:k}) =Lm,k(θ)p(θ∣m,𝒟0:k−1)cm,k.\displaystyle=\frac{L_{m,k}(\theta)\,p(\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D}_{0:k-1})}{c_{m,k}}. (34)

Initialize Z^m0\widehat{Z}_{m}^{0} and the parameter particles by tempered SMC on 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}. Given normalized retained weights Wm,ik−1W_{m,i}^{k-1}, evaluate only the new trajectory at each retained parameter value:

c^m,k\displaystyle\widehat{c}_{m,k} =∑i=1NpWm,ik−1​L^m,k​(θm,ik−1),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{p}}W_{m,i}^{k-1}\widehat{L}_{m,k}(\theta_{m,i}^{k-1}), log⁡Z^mk\displaystyle\log\widehat{Z}_{m}^{k} =log⁡Z^mk−1+log⁡c^m,k,\displaystyle=\log\widehat{Z}_{m}^{k-1}+\log\widehat{c}_{m,k}, (35)
W~m,ik\displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{m,i}^{k} =Wm,ik−1​L^m,k​(θm,ik−1)c^m,k.\displaystyle=\frac{W_{m,i}^{k-1}\widehat{L}_{m,k}(\theta_{m,i}^{k-1})}{\widehat{c}_{m,k}}. (36)

Here L^\widehat{L} is the exact likelihood when tractable, or its PF estimate for stochastic dynamics; the implementation computes the sums in log space. The model weights are then proportional to p⁡(m)​Z^mkp(m)\widehat{Z}_{m}^{k} over the current archive. If 1/∑i(W~m,ik)21/\sum_{i}(\widetilde{W}_{m,i}^{k})^{2} falls below Np/2N_{p}/2, we systematically resample parameter particles and reset their weights to 1/Np1/N_{p}, without changing the accumulated evidence. Otherwise we retain the weighted particles. The HH SDE+PF experiment in Section D.3 uses this procedure, with Np=64N_{p}=64 and Nz=128N_{z}=128, and no subsequent parameter rejuvenation.

Cost and limitations.

Excluding initialization, for fixed particle counts and no full-history rejuvenation, the recursive cost per model is O⁡(Np​∑k=1KC⁡(Tk))O(N_{p}\sum_{k=1}^{K}C(T_{k})), where C⁡(T)C(T) is the cost of one trajectory likelihood. For equal lengths and a tractable O⁡(T)O(T) likelihood, this is O⁡(K​T​Np)O(KTN_{p}) rather than O⁡(K2​T​Np)O(K^{2}TN_{p}); suppressing likelihood cost gives the O⁡(K​Np)O(KN_{p}) versus O⁡(K2​Np)O(K^{2}N_{p}) comparison. For PF, C⁡(T)=O⁡(T​Nz)C(T)=O(TN_{z}) at fixed solver resolution. Thus recursion avoids revisiting old experiments but does not eliminate the cost of processing a long new trajectory. For a single growing time series, analogous within-trajectory updates require retaining each parameter particle’s latent filtering state; the implemented HH outer update instead assimilates whole, independently initialized experiments.

Repeated resampling can collapse parameter diversity: it duplicates existing values rather than discovering new ones. The recursion is therefore a finite-particle approximation, not a guarantee of accurate long-run evidence. Weight ESS after resampling does not measure distinct parameter support; particle impoverishment can understate parameter uncertainty and distort both prediction intervals and acquisition scores. (See (Chopin, 2002; Chopin et al., 2013) for details.) Posterior-invariant MCMC rejuvenation or occasional batch refits can help, but may require evaluating the full history and invalidate the simple linear-cost bound. A newly proposed structure has no inherited parameter posterior or evidence and must be fitted on all accumulated data; the current HH implementation refits when the archive changes.

A.6.3 BIC approximation

As a faster alternative to tempered SMC, we use the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which we now explain.

Write ℓm​(θ)=log⁡p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ)\ell_{m}(\theta)=\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\theta) and Cm=dim(θm)C_{m}=\dim(\theta_{m}). For an interior maximum and a smooth prior, the large-sample Laplace approximation is

log⁡Zm≈ℓm​(θ^m)+log⁡p⁡(θ^m∣m)+Cm2​log⁡(2​π)−12​log​|Hm|,\log Z_{m}\approx\ell_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m})+\log p(\hat{\theta}_{m}\mid m)+\frac{C_{m}}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac{1}{2}\log|H_{m}|, (37)

where Hm=−∇2ℓm​(θ^m)H_{m}=-\nabla^{2}\ell_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m}). Under regularity conditions, HmH_{m} grows proportionally to NN, so retaining the leading terms gives

−2​log⁡Zm≈BICm=−2​ℓm​(θ^m)+Cm​log⁡N.-2\log Z_{m}\approx\mathrm{BIC}_{m}=-2\ell_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m})+C_{m}\log N. (38)

BIC drops bounded, generally model-dependent prior-density and curvature terms. We normalize p(m)exp(−BICm/2)p(m)\exp(-\mathrm{BIC}_{m}/2) over the candidate pool. Below we discuss how to compute BIC, with different noise assumptions. See Algorithm 8 for the pseudocode.

Fixed residual scale (τ=1\tau=1).

For NN scalar observations, assume fixed positive whitening scales σn\sigma_{n} shared across candidates, and define

RSSm​(θ)=∑n=1N(yn−y^n​(θ)σn)2.\mathrm{RSS}_{m}(\theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(\frac{y_{n}-\hat{y}_{n}(\theta)}{\sigma_{n}}\right)^{2}. (39)

With independent Gaussian errors and θ^m\hat{\theta}_{m} minimizing this RSS,

−2​log⁡p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ^m)=RSSm+∑n=1Nlog⁡(2​π​σn2).-2\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\hat{\theta}_{m})=\mathrm{RSS}_{m}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log(2\pi\sigma_{n}^{2}). (40)

For a common σn=σ\sigma_{n}=\sigma, the last term is N​log⁡(2​π​σ2)N\log(2\pi\sigma^{2}). This is the negative twice-log-likelihood, not yet BIC: adding the parameter penalty and dropping the shared normalization gives

BICmfixed=RSSm+Cm​log⁡N.\mathrm{BIC}^{\mathrm{fixed}}_{m}=\mathrm{RSS}_{m}+C_{m}\log N. (41)

Here RSSm=RSSm​(θ^m)\mathrm{RSS}_{m}=\mathrm{RSS}_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m}) is already noise-whitened.

Fitted (profiled) residual scale.

Alternatively, retain the same fixed whitening scales σn\sigma_{n}, shared across candidate models, and an unknown common residual-scale multiplier τ\tau, giving the log likelihood

yn|m,θm,τ\displaystyle y_{n}\mid m,\theta_{m},\tau ∼𝒩⁡(y^n​(θm),τ2​σn2),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{y}_{n}(\theta_{m}),\tau^{2}\sigma_{n}^{2}\right), (42)
−2​log⁡p⁡(𝒟∣m,θm,τ)\displaystyle-2\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\theta_{m},\tau) =RSSm​(θm)τ2+N​log⁡τ2+∑n=1Nlog⁡(2​π​σn2).\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}_{m}(\theta_{m})}{\tau^{2}}+N\log\tau^{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log(2\pi\sigma_{n}^{2}). (43)

The maximum-likelihood estimate θ^m\hat{\theta}_{m} minimizes this weighted RSS. Writing RSSm=RSSm​(θ^m)\mathrm{RSS}_{m}=\mathrm{RSS}_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m}), maximizing over τ\tau gives τ^m2=RSSm/N\hat{\tau}_{m}^{2}=\mathrm{RSS}_{m}/N. Substitution yields

−2​log⁡p⁡(𝒟∣m,θ^m,τ^m)=N​log⁡(RSSm/N)+N+∑n=1Nlog⁡(2​π​σn2).-2\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid m,\hat{\theta}_{m},\hat{\tau}_{m})=N\log(\mathrm{RSS}_{m}/N)+N+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log(2\pi\sigma_{n}^{2}). (44)

The full BIC adds (Cm+1)​log⁡N(C_{m}+1)\log N, since the fitted scale τ\tau is one additional parameter. The terms NN and ∑nlog⁡(2​π​σn2)\sum_{n}\log(2\pi\sigma_{n}^{2}) and this additional log⁡N\log N are identical for every candidate on the same dataset, so we drop them. This gives the comparison score

BICm\displaystyle\mathrm{BIC}_{m} :=N​log⁡(RSSm/N)+Cm​log⁡N.\displaystyle:=N\log(\mathrm{RSS}_{m}/N)+C_{m}\log N. (45)

where Cm=dim(θm)C_{m}=\dim(\theta_{m}) is the number of fitted model parameters (excluding the common fitted residual scale). Lower is better. We use logZ^m=−BICm/2\log\widehat{Z}_{m}=-\mathrm{BIC}_{m}/2 as an approximate evidence score, and normalize p(m)exp(−BICm/2)p(m)\exp(-\mathrm{BIC}_{m}/2) over the pool.

Noise terms σn\sigma_{n}.

The term σn\sigma_{n} is a heteroscedastic whitening scale:

σn\displaystyle\sigma_{n} =max⁡(ρ​|yn|,σfloor)\displaystyle=\max\!\left(\rho|y_{n}|,\sigma_{\mathrm{floor}}\right) (46)

In ChemBench we use ρ=0.03\rho=0.03 and σfloor=0.01\sigma_{\mathrm{floor}}=0.01. For the stochastic HH experiment, the deterministic ODE+BIC control instead uses a constant σn=2​mV\sigma_{n}=2\,\mathrm{mV} (equivalently, ρ=0\rho=0 and σfloor=2​mV\sigma_{\mathrm{floor}}=2\,\mathrm{mV}), matching the declared voltage observation noise. Each trajectory contributes 20 voltage observations, so N=20​(N0+k)N=20(N_{0}+k) after kk active experiments and N0N_{0} initial trajectories.

Comparison of BIC estimators.

In the end-to-end ChemBench control in Fig. 7, fixed-scale BIC gives better early-budget predictions than profiled-scale BIC under CMA-EIG, although their performance is similar at 15 observations.

A.7 Prior sensitivity

The model evidence averages the likelihood over the parameter prior, rather than only rewarding its maximum. A diffuse prior can therefore strongly penalize a model even when its fitted predictions barely change (Llorente et al., 2022). For example, enlarging a uniform prior’s volume by a factor cc, while leaving the likelihood integral essentially unchanged, reduces log⁡Zm\log Z_{m} by log⁡c\log c; an improper prior leaves ordinary Bayes factors undefined.

In Eq. 37, BIC retains the leading terms ℓm​(θ^m)−12​Cm​log⁡N\ell_{m}(\hat{\theta}_{m})-\tfrac{1}{2}C_{m}\log N, dropping prior-density and curvature terms that can matter at small NN. It avoids explicit prior-volume normalization, but fitting bounds still matter, and unidentified parameters violate its regularity assumptions. Thus a predictive advantage for BIC need not mean that it estimates evidence more accurately. Figure 7 compares predictive performance of complete inference configurations; it does not isolate evidence-estimation accuracy.

A.8 Computing the model posterior

The main inference procedure over models, given the current hypothesis class ℳ\mathcal{M}, is shown in Algorithm 9. This just applies Bayes rule to compute p⁡(m∣𝒟)p(m\mid\mathcal{D}) for each m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, and then keeps the top NmN_{m} candidates.

ℳ\mathcal{M}-open extension.

When the current best (MAP) model’s residual (error) e∗e^{*} exceeds a threshold τe\tau_{e} (Algorithm 13), we invoke expand-hyp-space (Algorithm 12): the LLM proposes a batch of NnewN_{\mathrm{new}} new structures from the observations and available fit diagnostics. ChemBench provides residuals for the current pool, inspired by the pool-conditioned proposals of SMC-S (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024); glucose supplies observed trajectories and candidate fit diagnostics. The new structures are scored by evidence and the pool is evidence-pruned in the following model-posterior call. If e∗≤τee^{*}\leq\tau_{e} the pool is left unchanged and model-posterior merely re-scores the existing structures on the new datum — no LLM call.

The predictive check.

The predictive check measures how well the current model explains observations; a large discrepancy triggers ℳ\mathcal{M}-open expansion. Algorithm 13 gives a prequential variant: score the new observation before fitting it, optionally combining this with residuals on stored data. The executed ChemBench and DP agents instead gate their first expansion on residuals cached from the preceding fit. They then refit on all available data and, if expanding again, recheck that fit. A newly surprising observation can therefore affect expansion one update later. Neither version retains a running archive of historical forecasts. Relative residuals balance component scales, and taking their median limits the influence of outliers, but can also delay expansion after a single informative failure. More precisely, let the relative error on experiment jj be the median relative error over target components ii:

rj​(m,θ)\displaystyle r_{j}(m,\theta) =median𝑖​|Fi(yj)−𝔼[Fi(Y)∣χj,m,θ]|max⁡(|Fi​(yj)|,ci)\displaystyle=\underset{i}{\operatorname{median}}\frac{\left|F_{i}(y_{j})-\mathbb{E}[F_{i}(Y)\mid\chi_{j},m,\theta]\right|}{\max\!\left(\left|F_{i}(y_{j})\right|,c_{i}\right)} (47)

Then the estimated error at step kk is

e∗\displaystyle e^{*} =median⁡({rk​(m∗,θ^m∗)}∪{rj​(m∗,θ^m∗):j<k}𝚋𝚊𝚌𝚔𝚝𝚎𝚜𝚝),\displaystyle=\operatorname{median}\left(\{r_{k}(m^{*},\hat{\theta}^{m^{*}})\}\cup\{r_{j}(m^{*},\hat{\theta}^{m^{*}}):j<k\}_{\mathtt{backtest}}\right), (48)

where the first set is the prequential error on the new observation and the optional second set contains the back-test errors. Here m∗m^{*} and θ^m∗\hat{\theta}^{m^{*}} are fixed at their pre-observation values when the new datum is scored. Expansion is triggered when e∗>τee^{*}>\tau_{e}.

Finite-pool interpretation and limitations.

The outer (model inference) loop, at step kk, is approximating the following target distribution

pk​(m)∝p⁡(m)​Zm(k)p_{k}(m)\ \propto\ p(m)\,Z_{m}^{(k)} (49)

On a deduplicated finite pool ℳ\mathcal{M}, exact evidences would give the restricted posterior wi∝p⁡(mi)​Zmi(k)w_{i}\propto p(m_{i})Z_{m_{i}}^{(k)}. In practice the evidences, or their BIC substitutes, are approximate. When enabled, residual-conditioned LLM proposals enlarge this support (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024); top-NmN_{m} pruning is deterministic hypothesis search, not a posterior-invariant resampling kernel. Normalizing over enumerated unique candidates does not require treating them as importance samples from the LLM, but it also does not account for unproposed model mass.

A.9 Algorithms for experiment design

VoI API.

The design step maximises a VoI score over the design space. Algorithm 14 defines the interface, which reads off the pooled two-level posterior p⁡(m∣𝒟)​Wimp(m\mid\mathcal{D})\,W_{i}^{m}. The objectives only differ in which uncertainty they reduce — the model index (model-discrimination EIG, the default), or the whole latent (m,θ)(m,\theta) (joint EIG). We derive these objectives below.

From Value of information to expected information gain.

The VoI, first proposed in (Howard, 1966), is a decision-theoretic concept defined as follows: for a terminal decision d∈Δd\in\Delta with utility U⁡(a,h)U(a,h) over the unknown state of nature hh, the value of running experiment χ\chi is the expected gain in attainable utility from observing its outcome before deciding,

VoIU(χ)=𝔼y∼p(⋅∣χ,𝒟)[maxd∈Δ𝔼p⁡(h∣𝒟,y,χ)U(d,h)]−maxd∈Δ𝔼p⁡(h∣𝒟)U(d,h),\mathrm{VoI}_{U}(\chi)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(\cdot\mid\chi,\mathcal{D})}\Big[\,\max_{d\in\Delta}\ \mathbb{E}_{p(h\mid\mathcal{D},y,\chi)}\,U(d,h)\,\Big]\;-\;\max_{d\in\Delta}\ \mathbb{E}_{p(h\mid\mathcal{D})}\,U(d,h), (50)

measured in the units of the task utility UU.

Now let the decision be model identification, i.e. report a distribution q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) over the model index h=mh=m under the log score U⁡(q,m)=log⁡q⁡(m)U(q,m)=\log q(m). The inner maximiser is the posterior, q⋆=p⁡(M∣𝒟,y,χ)q^{\star}=p(M\mid\mathcal{D},y,\chi), and maxq𝔼p(M∣⋅)logq(M)=−H[p(M∣⋅)]\max_{q}\mathbb{E}_{p(M\mid\cdot)}\log q(M)=-H[p(M\mid\cdot)], so Eq. 50 becomes

VoIlog​(χ)=(−𝔼y​H​[p⁡(M∣𝒟,y,χ)])−(−H⁡[p⁡(M∣𝒟)])=I⁡(M;Yχ∣𝒟)=EIG⁡(χ).\mathrm{VoI}_{\log}(\chi)=\Big(-\,\mathbb{E}_{y}\,H[p(M\mid\mathcal{D},y,\chi)]\Big)-\Big(-H[p(M\mid\mathcal{D})]\Big)=I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})=\mathrm{EIG}(\chi). (51)

This is known as the Expected information gain (EIG), and was first proposed by (Lindley, 1956). (We discuss other forms of VoI below.)

Estimating the EIG.

We estimate the EIG as follows. First we rewrite the mutual information of Eq. 51 in its outcome-entropy form, I(M;Yχ∣𝒟)=H[Yχ∣𝒟]−H[Yχ∣M,𝒟]I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})=H[Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D}]-H[Y_{\chi}\mid M,\mathcal{D}], in terms of each structure’s posterior predictive of the outcome,

Pm​(⋅):=p⁡(Yχ∣m,𝒟,χ)=∫p⁡(Yχ∣m,θ,χ)​p​(θ∣m,𝒟)​𝑑θ,P_{m}(\cdot)\;:=\;p\big(Y_{\chi}\mid m,\mathcal{D},\chi\big)\;=\;\int p\big(Y_{\chi}\mid m,\theta,\chi\big)\,p(\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D})\,d\theta, (52)

i.e. the distribution of the outcome we would observe under design χ\chi if structure mm were true, with its parameters marginalised over the within-structure posterior. Writing p⁡(m):=p⁡(m∣𝒟)p(m):=p(m\mid\mathcal{D}), the marginal predictive is the mixture p⁡(Yχ∣𝒟)=∑mp⁡(m)​Pmp(Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})=\sum_{m}p(m)\,P_{m}, so H⁡[Yχ∣𝒟]=H⁡(∑mp⁡(m)​Pm)H[Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D}]=H\!\big(\sum_{m}p(m)P_{m}\big); and conditioning on M=mM{=}m makes Yχ∼PmY_{\chi}\sim P_{m}, so H[Yχ∣M,𝒟]=∑mp(m)H(Pm)H[Y_{\chi}\mid M,\mathcal{D}]=\sum_{m}p(m)\,H(P_{m}). Hence

EIG​(χ)=I⁡(M;Yχ∣𝒟)=H⁡(∑mp⁡(m)​Pm)−∑mp⁡(m)​H​(Pm).\text{EIG}(\chi)\;=\;I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})\;=\;H\!\Big(\sum_{m}p(m)\,P_{m}\Big)\;-\;\sum_{m}p(m)\,H(P_{m}). (53)

The first term is the entropy of the mixture predictive (the total uncertainty about the outcome); the second is the average entropy within a structure (the irreducible outcome noise that cannot help discriminate MM). Their difference is the outcome uncertainty attributable to not knowing which structure is true — equivalently I(M;Yχ∣𝒟)=∑mp(m)KL(Pm∥∑m′p(m′)Pm′)I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})=\sum_{m}p(m)\,\operatorname{KL}\!\big(P_{m}\,\big\|\,\sum_{m^{\prime}}p(m^{\prime})P_{m^{\prime}}\big), the mean KL from each structure’s predictive to the mixture (a generalised Jensen–Shannon divergence), which is manifestly maximised by designs χ\chi that drive the PmP_{m} apart.

Gaussian approximation.

The MI is intractable for general mixture, so we specialise to a Gaussian likelihood model and use a deterministic moment-matching approximation. Let Yχ∈ℝdY_{\chi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the quantity the likelihood conditions on, which could be the raw trace y1:Ty_{1:T} or some summary. Model its outcome, conditional on the model mm, as Yχm=μ¯m​(χ)+εY^{m}_{\chi}=\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi)+\varepsilon, where

μ¯m​(χ)\displaystyle\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi) =𝔼θ|m,𝒟[𝔼[Yχ∣m,θ,χ]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[Y_{\chi}\mid m,\theta,\chi]\right] (54)

and ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σε)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\varepsilon}) is an assumed common within-model noise covariance (σ2​I\sigma^{2}I in the simplest case). Parameter and process uncertainty generally make the actual within-model predictive covariance model-dependent; the following bound applies to this common-covariance surrogate model, not automatically to the original mixture. The unconditional distribution is thus the Gaussian mixture

Yχ∼∑mp⁡(m∣𝒟)​𝒩​(μ¯m​(χ),Σε)\displaystyle Y_{\chi}\sim\sum_{m}p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\,\mathcal{N}(\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi),\Sigma_{\varepsilon}) (55)

with covariance Σε+Σμ​(χ)\Sigma_{\varepsilon}+\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi), where Σμ​(χ)=Varp⁡(m∣𝒟)⁡[μ¯m​(χ)]\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi)=\operatorname{Var}_{p(m\mid\mathcal{D})}[\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi)] is the d×dd\times d between-class covariance of the mean predictions. The conditional entropy H⁡[Yχ∣M]=12​ln⁡((2​π​e)d​detΣε)H[Y_{\chi}\mid M]=\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\!\big((2\pi e)^{d}\det\Sigma_{\varepsilon}\big) is exact, but a Gaussian mixture has no closed-form differential entropy, so we approximate H⁡[Yχ]H[Y_{\chi}] by the entropy of a single Gaussian of the same covariance (moment matching). The (2​π​e)d​detΣε(2\pi e)^{d}\det\Sigma_{\varepsilon} cancels in the difference, giving

I⁡(M;Yχ∣𝒟)=H⁡[Yχ]−H⁡[Yχ∣M]≈12​ln​det(I+Σε−1​Σμ​(χ)),I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})=H[Y_{\chi}]-H[Y_{\chi}\mid M]\approx\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\det\!\Big(I+\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi)\Big), (56)

In the scalar case d=1d{=}1, this becomes

I⁡(M;Yχ∣𝒟)≈12​ln⁡(1+Var⁡[μ⁡(χ)]/σ2)I(M;Y_{\chi}\mid\mathcal{D})\approx\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1+\operatorname{Var}[\mu(\chi)]/\sigma^{2}) (57)

This is an upper bound on the true mutual information, since a Gaussian maximises entropy at fixed covariance. Furthermore, it is monotone (in the Loewner order1111 11 The Loewner (partial) order on symmetric matrices: A⪰BA\succeq B iff A−BA-B is positive semidefinite (Pukelsheim, 2006). With the same noise covariance at both designs, Σμ​(χ)⪰Σμ​(χ′)\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi)\succeq\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi^{\prime}) implies Eq. 56 is at least as large at χ\chi, so a design that raises the between-class covariance in every direction has a no-smaller surrogate score. For design-dependent noise, compare noise-whitened covariances instead.) in the between-class covariance Σμ​(χ)\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi). This makes it a principled surrogate — a design that raises the between-class covariance can only raise the score — although, since different designs generally induce incomparable covariances under the Loewner order, we do not claim its arg⁡max\arg\max exactly coincides with that of the true mixture mutual information.

Weighted model disagreement.

A cheaper surrogate replaces the log-determinant by the trace of Σε−1​Σμ​(χ)\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi). This resembles information-matrix criteria in optimal design (Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995; Pukelsheim, 2006), but is not itself a posterior ellipsoid volume or exact mutual information for a categorical model index. Unlike EIG, which is bounded by H⁡(M∣𝒟)H(M\mid\mathcal{D}), this trace can be arbitrarily large. In practice, we therefore use the following

χ⋆\displaystyle\chi^{\star} =arg⁡maxχ∈𝒳​tr⁡(Σε−1​Σμ​(χ))\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\chi\in\mathcal{X}}\ \operatorname{tr}\!\big(\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}\Sigma_{\mu}(\chi)\big) (58)
=arg⁡max⁡∑mχ⁡p⁡(m∣𝒟)​∥μ¯m​(χ)−μ¯​(χ)∥Σε−12,\displaystyle=\arg\max_{\chi}\ \textstyle\sum_{m}p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\,\big\lVert\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi)-\bar{\mu}(\chi)\big\rVert^{2}_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}}, (59)
μ¯m​(χ)\displaystyle\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi) =𝔼θ|m,𝒟[𝔼[Yχ∣m,θ,χ]]≈∑iWimμm,θmi(χ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\mid m,\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}[Y_{\chi}\mid m,\theta,\chi]\right]\approx\sum_{i}W_{i}^{m}\mu_{m,\theta_{m}^{i}}(\chi) (60)
μ¯​(χ)\displaystyle\bar{\mu}(\chi) =∑mp⁡(m∣𝒟)​μ¯m​(χ)\displaystyle=\sum_{m}p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\,\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi) (61)

where ∥v∥A2=v⊤​A​v\lVert v\rVert^{2}_{A}{=}v^{\top}Av, and we have assumed the parameter posterior is represented as a set of weighted samples, p⁡(θ|m,𝒟)=∑iWim​δ​(θ−θmi)p(\theta|m,\mathcal{D})=\sum_{i}W_{i}^{m}\delta(\theta-\theta_{m}^{i}). (Note that using per-class means μ¯m​(χ)\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi) rather than noisy draws keeps EIG genuine epistemic disagreement — Lindley’s intuition (Lindley, 1956) that the best experiment is the one whose outcome current beliefs least agree on.)

Why moment-matching rather than nested Monte Carlo.

With a finite model pool and exact conditional predictive densities, an unbiased outer Monte Carlo estimator of EIG is:

EIG^​(χ)=1N​∑n=1Nlog⁡p⁡(yn∣mn,χ)∑m′p⁡(m′∣𝒟)​p​(yn∣m′,χ),mn∼p⁡(m∣𝒟),yn∼p⁡(Yχ∣mn,𝒟),\widehat{\mathrm{EIG}}(\chi)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log\frac{p(y_{n}\mid m_{n},\chi)}{\sum_{m^{\prime}}p(m^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{D})\,p(y_{n}\mid m^{\prime},\chi)},\qquad m_{n}\sim p(m\mid\mathcal{D}),\ \ y_{n}\sim p(Y_{\chi}\mid m_{n},\mathcal{D}), (62)

where the inner sum is the marginal predictive p⁡(yn∣χ,𝒟)p(y_{n}\mid\chi,\mathcal{D}). (A further inner loop over the particles θ\theta appears when parameters are not marginalised analytically). This is the estimator BoxingGym’s info_gain evaluates. The displayed estimator is unbiased under those assumptions. Approximating the conditional densities inside the logarithm introduces additional finite-inner-sample bias; that nested approximation is distinct from the outer Monte Carlo error. The finite-model sum costs O⁡(N​|ℳ|)O(N\lvert\mathcal{M}\rvert) per candidate design (Rainforth et al., 2024; Foster et al., 2021). This yields a noisy, slow, non-smooth objective for the design search, which is why we maximise the fast, closed-form surrogate Eq. 59 instead.

EIG for model and parameters.

An alternative acquisition keeps the within-class parameter spread instead of averaging it out. By the law of total variance the full two-level predictive variance splits into the between-class term of Eq. (59) plus a within-class one:

tr⁡(Σε−1​Varp⁡(m,θ∣𝒟)​[𝔼⁡(Yχ∣m,θ,do⁡(χ))])\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}\!\Big(\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}\operatorname{Var}_{p(m,\theta\mid\mathcal{D})}\!\big[\,\mathbb{E}(Y_{\chi}\mid m,\theta,\mathrm{do}(\chi))\,\big]\Big) =∑mp⁡(m∣𝒟)​∥μ¯m​(χ)−μ¯​(χ)∥Σε−12⏟between classes (mechanism disagreement)\displaystyle=\underbrace{\sum_{m}p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\big\lVert\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi)-\bar{\mu}(\chi)\big\rVert^{2}_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}}}_{\text{between classes (mechanism disagreement)}}
+∑mp⁡(m∣𝒟)​∑iWim​∥μm,i​(χ)−μ¯m​(χ)∥Σε−12⏟within class (parameter uncertainty),\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\sum_{m}p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\sum_{i}W_{i}^{m}\big\lVert\mu_{m,i}(\chi)-\bar{\mu}_{m}(\chi)\big\rVert^{2}_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}}}_{\text{within class (parameter uncertainty)}}, (63)

estimated empirically by the pooled particle variance ∑m,iwm,i​∥μm,i​(χ)−μ¯​(χ)∥Σε−12\sum_{m,i}w_{m,i}\big\lVert\mu_{m,i}(\chi)-\bar{\mu}(\chi)\big\rVert^{2}_{\Sigma_{\varepsilon}^{-1}} with wm,i∝p⁡(m∣𝒟)​Wimw_{m,i}\!\propto\!p(m\mid\mathcal{D})\,W_{i}^{m}. Only the between-class term is collapsed by identifying the class. The within-class term is residual parameter uncertainty. If the per-structure parameter posteriors have concentrated, this latter term becomes negligible, so this full variance coincides with Eq. (59). However, optimizing Eq. 63 can be useful if the parameter values contain more useful information than just the model index. (We tried this version in Section E.6, but found it to be less numerically stable than Eq. 59.)

Optimising over a large design space.

When the design space is large, we can use various gradient free optimizers to pick the design. For continuous spaces a common choice is CMA-ES (Hansen, 2016). For discrete spaces, we can use LLM-driven evolutionary search methods such as FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024).

From model-discrimination to task-aware design.

So far we have assumed the goal is to identify the true model, so we have optimized EIG I⁡(M,Yχ)I(M;Y_{\chi}), spending budget to resolve which structure generated the data. But since we ultimately evaluate performance in terms of prediction accuracy of a target variable, we only need to resolve the model to the extent that it changes the forecast of the target FF on the query distribution 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.
